In [[mathematics]], in the field of [[group theory]], a [[group (mathematics)|group]] is said to be '''absolutely simple''' if it has no proper nontrivial [[serial subgroup]]s.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Robinson | first = Derek J. S.
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4419-8594-1
 | edition = Second
 | isbn = 0-387-94461-3
 | location = New York
 | mr = 1357169
 | page = 381
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = Graduate Texts in Mathematics
 | title = A course in the theory of groups
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=lqyCjUFY6WAC&pg=PA381
 | volume = 80
 | year = 1996}}.</ref> That is, <math>G</math> is an absolutely simple group if the only serial subgroups of <math>G</math> are <math>\{ e \}</math> (the trivial subgroup), and <math>G</math> itself (the whole group).

In the finite case, a group is absolutely simple if and only if it is [[simple group|simple]]. However, in the infinite case, absolutely simple is a stronger property than simple. The property of being strictly simple is somewhere in between.
